opus-5.5.text:
Looking back, VTA was one of the more fun and, honestly, slightly crazy things we did in the early days of TVM. The motivation was pretty simple. We were building a compiler stack that claimed to target many kinds of hardware, CPUs, GPUs, and eventually specialized accelerators. But at the time, most accelerators were closed. You couldn't really see inside them, and you certainly couldn't co-design the software and the hardware together. So we asked ourselves: if we really believe the compiler should be able to handle new hardware, why don't we build an open accelerator ourselves and use it to stress-test the whole stack?

That was the spirit behind VTA. It wasn't meant to be the fastest chip in the world. It was meant to be a vehicle for research, a minimal but realistic template that captured the essential ideas of deep learning accelerators: a tensor compute core for things like matrix multiplication, explicit on-chip memory buffers, load and store modules, and a decoupled access-execute style so that memory movement and compute could overlap. We kept the instruction set small and explicit, so that the compiler had to take responsibility for scheduling, tiling, and managing latency. That was really the point. We wanted to push the complexity into software and see whether the compiler could handle it.

A big lesson for me was how much hardware and software design are really the same problem viewed from two sides. When you design the hardware, every decision about buffer sizes or synchronization becomes a constraint the compiler has to reason about. And when you build the compiler, you start to see which hardware features actually matter and which ones are just nice on paper. Having the whole thing open, from the high-level model down to the FPGA bitstream, let us iterate on both sides very quickly. That kind of end-to-end loop is something I still value a lot.

It was also a great collaboration. People coming from the architecture side and people coming from the systems and machine learning side had to learn each other's language. I think that cross-pollination ended up influencing how TVM itself evolved, things like how we think about tensorization, memory scopes, and making the compiler extensible enough to plug in new hardware backends.

So when I look back, I see VTA less as a chip and more as an argument. It was a way of demonstrating that an open, automated compiler stack can and should be part of how we design new hardware, not something bolted on at the end. And I think that idea, hardware–software co-design with machine learning compilers at the center, has only become more important since then.

r002.rationale: It connects the small, explicit instruction set to the compiler team's perspective: the compiler was expected to handle scheduling, tiling, and latency.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, VTA really came out of a frustration we had with the software side. When we were building TVM, we kept running into this wall where every accelerator we wanted to target was either a black box, a closed vendor design, or something we couldn't fully reason about end to end. If you want a compiler stack to generate good code for hardware, you need to understand what the hardware is actually doing, down to the instruction set and the memory hierarchy. And we just didn't have that.

So the motivation for VTA was less "let's build the fastest accelerator" and much more "let's build an accelerator that is transparent, parameterizable, and designed hand in hand with the compiler." Thierry Moreau drove a lot of the hardware side of that, and the whole point was to make the design simple enough that you could see every layer, from the TVM scheduling primitives down to the micro-ops running on the FPGA.

A few design choices still feel right to me. One was making the instruction set fairly decoupled, so you have explicit load, compute, and store modules with dependency queues between them. That let the compiler handle latency hiding through software pipelining rather than burying everything in hardware control logic. Another was exposing parameters like the GEMM tile shape and the buffer sizes, so you could regenerate different variants and explore the design space with the compiler in the loop rather than treating hardware as fixed.

If I'm honest about the limitations, VTA was never going to compete with a commercial chip on raw performance, and we were clear about that. The FPGA targets were modest. What it gave us was a full-stack research vehicle. Students could change the compiler, change the ISA, change the hardware, and measure the effect of all three together. That kind of co-design loop was really hard to get anywhere else at the time.

The other thing I'd say in hindsight is that it shaped how I think about abstractions in TVM more broadly. Working on VTA forced us to think about tensorization, about how you map a high-level operator onto a hardware intrinsic, and about how much of the scheduling the compiler should own versus the hardware. A lot of what later became the tensor program abstractions in TVM Unity and the way we think about hardware intrinsics traces back to lessons from that project. So even where VTA itself didn't become a widely deployed accelerator, the ideas carried forward.

astra-6.text:
Looking back, VTA was really a way for us to explore hardware and software together. In the early days of TVM, we were asking how a compiler could support specialized accelerators, but it was difficult to explore that question if the hardware was a black box. We wanted something small and open, where we could understand—and change—both sides.

The interesting part was the feedback loop. You might start with a hardware design that looks reasonable, then try to map a workload onto it and discover that data movement or synchronization makes the compiler’s job very difficult. That pushes you to rethink the interface, and sometimes the hardware itself.

So I think of VTA less as an attempt to build the ultimate accelerator and more as a vehicle for learning about that interface. The biggest lesson for me was that you can’t design the hardware in isolation and assume the software will figure everything out afterward. Working through the whole stack is what reveals which ideas actually fit together.

sol-6.1.text:
Looking back, I think the most interesting part was the interaction between the hardware and the compiler. With TVM, we were trying to understand how to support different hardware backends, and VTA gave us a concrete way to explore that question from both sides.

The goal wasn’t simply to build a faster accelerator. We wanted something small enough to understand end to end, but realistic enough that we had to deal with computation, data movement, and memory management together. When you make those things explicit, you start to see which decisions belong in the hardware and which decisions the compiler can handle.

That’s how I think about the design process: an opportunity for hardware and software to inform each other. The value was as much in what we learned about building that whole stack as in the accelerator itself.
